rows.title: Passengers were stuck because United canceled their flights. The airline’s CEO took a private plane to Denver.
rows.standfirst: “Taking a private jet was the wrong decision,” Scott Kirby said

rows.title: After internment, Japanese Americans took to farming in rural Colorado. Now, their legacies are at risk of fading.
rows.standfirst: Japanese American farmers built multigenerational businesses in Colorado after WWII and decades later, economic hardships make it difficult for them to stay afloat.

rows.title: Human-rights movement comes to Colorado with promise of more protections, rights for farmworkers
rows.standfirst: Beginning this season, Rancho Durazno in Palisade is the first agricultural enterprise in Colorado to join the Fair Food Program, an innovative human-rights movement that began a dozen years ago in Florida’s vast tomato fields.

rows.title: An entrepreneur is one big step closer to capturing methane leaking from Colorado coal mines
rows.standfirst: White River National Forest district ranger calls Coal Basin mine project “precedent setting”

rows.title: A leaky oil well poisoned a Colorado rancher’s herd, killing 6 cows. He still hasn’t been paid back.
rows.standfirst: Rancher says his yearslong dispute with Denver-based Western Operating Co. shows lack of accountability when oil and gas companies make mistakes

rows.title: Troubled Colorado oil and gas operator dodges cleanup deadline, $2M in fines as judge halts state enforcement action
rows.standfirst: K.P. Kauffman was supposed to pay its fines and remediate 78 sites by Aug. 1 or stop operating in Colorado. A judge agreed to stay that order while the company sues to block it from taking effect.

rows.title: Iconic Crystal Mill closes visitor trail after repeated bad behavior in the backcountry
rows.standfirst: Owners and local businesses blame Instagram for the influx of people who disregard leave no trace etiquette

rows.title: Colorado company seeking to mine Nebraska for rare earth minerals needed in EVs signs deal with carmaker
rows.standfirst: Centennial-based NioCorp announces tentative deal as it secure $1.1 billion need to establish mine 80 miles south of Omaha

rows.title: Colorado-based company has first commercially available “smart guns” for sale in U.S.
rows.standfirst: Biofire in Broomfield has produced a gun that can only be used by someone with the right fingerprint or face scan. Experts have differing visions of what a post-smart gun world might look like.

rows.title: What’s Working: Inflation in rural Colorado is likely higher than it is in the Denver area
rows.standfirst: The standard measure of inflation is only calculated for Denver and not the rest of the state. But here’s one new methodology.

rows.title: Rural Colorado to benefit from $85 million for workforce development — including nursing resources — amid shortage
rows.standfirst: Colorado needs thousands more nurses a year to keep up with growing demand amid staffing shortages and retirements in the health care workforce. But a $1.3 million grant to the Colorado State University Pueblo graduate school and nursing program as part of an $85 million state project is intended to keep adequate health care flowing […]

rows.title: Bluebird Backcountry will shut down its operations after pioneering an uphill-skiing resort model in Colorado
rows.standfirst: Bluebird’s founders are closing the lift-free ski area after four seasons at two remote locations

rows.title: Xcel Energy seeks $45M rate increase — down from $312M — amid consumer outrage over rising bills
rows.standfirst: The state’s largest utility slashed its request by 85%, but consumer advocates are troubled Xcel wants to tack shareholder returns, lawyer fees, employee bonuses onto customer bills

rows.title: Tiny homes starting to be a big-deal solution for people priced out of Colorado’s housing market
rows.standfirst: New state law puts tiny homes on the same regulatory foundation as other manufactured housing, opening the door to let people live in them long term

rows.title: Landlord twice sued by tenants in Aurora faces resident uprising at separate complex in Lakewood
rows.standfirst: People living in the Reed Apartments just west of Sloan Lake are getting help from a rising tenant advocacy group fighting for their landlord to fix problems with heat, plumbing and pest infestations

rows.title: Unhoused Coloradans turn to methamphetamine as a form of protection
rows.standfirst: In Colorado Springs, meth accounts for majority of drug overdose deaths. Many of the deceased were living outside, using the drug to stay awake.

rows.title: What’s Working: Job openings in Colorado decline as employers presumably find the staff they need
rows.standfirst: Job openings are in decline nationwide, too. Have we reached a new equilibrium? Plus: Who stopped looking for work?

rows.title: A food hall is bringing Pueblo’s “beautiful building stock” back to life. It’s just the start.
rows.standfirst: Fuel & Iron Food Hall has taken a community-focused approach by adding on-site workforce housing. The project is helping revitalize the city’s historic downtown.

rows.title: When Taylor Swift came to Denver she brought a spectacle and left a $140 million economic afterglow
rows.standfirst: But pop superstar Taylor Swift’s Eras tour isn’t just about the money. It’s also about friendship bracelets, handmade outfits, and connecting with fans from around the world

rows.title: Colorado is shutting down insurer Friday Health Plans, impacting more than 30,000 people
rows.standfirst: The move means people currently covered by the insurer will need to find new health care coverage this summer

rows.title: Colorado property owners file record number of protests with county assessors who set new taxation values
rows.standfirst: The number of protests filed with Colorado’s 64 county assessors increased 300% in 2023 compared to the average number of protests from the previous three assessment cycles.

rows.title: Coloradans increasingly concerned about cost of living, housing and homelessness, poll shows
rows.standfirst: Data from the Colorado Health Foundation’s annual poll shows concerns over housing increased — just as Denver’s new mayor declares state of emergency over homelessness

rows.title: A Denver bookstore’s gift registry lets strangers buy books for classrooms
rows.standfirst: The Bookies Bookstore has gifted 1,500 books and counting to teachers across the state as many can’t afford to refresh their classroom libraries

rows.title: President and CEO at Central City Opera out in the middle of the company’s summer festival
rows.standfirst: The opera company’s board hired Pamela Pantos to the role in February 2022. She left the organization after a monthslong labor dispute between arts workers and management.

rows.title: Tiny spill of water likely tainted with uranium in Cañon City confirms watchdog group’s worries about Superfund site cleanup
rows.standfirst: State health officials say Cotter Corp., which ran a uranium milling operation there for decades, will return to manage the site until cleanup is complete

rows.title: Experiment to pay Denver’s homeless has reached $5 million and 846 people
rows.standfirst: Six months in, there are not yet concrete results in the yearlong study, but organizers report that the payments have been life altering for some

rows.title: What’s driving sudden flare of solar energy and storage in Colorado?
rows.standfirst: A slew of new projects spotlights state’s leadership in renewable policy and economics, experts say

rows.title: Colorado is first in the U.S. to make rules tying pollution reduction to oil and gas production
rows.standfirst: The “emissions intensity” rule requires companies closely monitor methane releases and limits allowed pollution based on how much oil and gas they produce

rows.title: What’s Working: Denver still a top 10 city for tech, thanks to tech wages outpacing rent growth
rows.standfirst: There’s other factors, including the number of young, educated and tech-savvy workers. Plus: “Durable skills” vs. AI, Colorado’s June job report and more!

rows.title: As Colorado’s electric vehicle charging infrastructure grows, the question remains: Who will pay for it?
rows.standfirst: Private companies are already making major investments in EV charging. But should monopoly utilities, like Xcel, support them or build their own?

rows.title: Denver’s homeless population grew 31.7% in one year, annual survey finds
rows.standfirst: As COVID-19 relief funds and rental assistance end, human service providers say the number of people who are homeless has increased

rows.title: While EV sales have flattened in Colorado, sales for alternative-fuel cars keep rising
rows.standfirst: EV sales flattened a bit in 2Q despite price cuts, but sales of hybrid RAV-4s and CRVs boost alternative cars

rows.title: Here’s how you can help those most in need in Colorado by getting rid of your old stuff
rows.standfirst: A number of organizations collect stuff Coloradans no longer want. Here are a handful that turned it into a business that in turn helps folks who have trouble finding work.

rows.title: Colorado affordable housing advocates urge local governments to opt into Proposition 123. Only 14 have applied for funding so far.
rows.standfirst: The success of the ballot measure hinges on participation from local governments, which must commit to increasing their affordable housing stock by 3% every year for the next three-year cycle of the program.

rows.title: Tiny worms have infested up to 40% of Colorado’s Olathe Sweet corn crop
rows.standfirst: Tuxedo, the state’s largest sweet corn producer, is only packing about 3,000 crates per day for shipment to stores compared with three times that in a normal year

rows.title: Home sweet parking lot: Some hospitals welcome RV living for patients, families and workers
rows.standfirst: At the hospital in Salida, doctors and nurses commuting from distant cities are more likely than patients to camp in the parking lot

rows.title: Colorado tourism still impacted by COVID-19 and inflation, new report shows
rows.standfirst: The state reached a record high of $27.7 billion in travel spending and 90 million visitors in 2022, as it continues to feel the “aftershocks” of the pandemic

rows.title: What’s Working: Where to get rid of hard-to-toss items in Colorado — and also benefit society
rows.standfirst: From old couches and mattresses to baby gear, paint and contact lenses, these Colorado organizations want your old stuff to help the planet, consumers and an underused workforce.
